analysis.one_liner: Treats U.S. companies that redomicile offshore to escape U.S. taxes as domestic corporations.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Rep. Richard Neal with 10 Democratic cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died in the House Ways and Means Committee when Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: When a U.S. company technically reorganizes so a foreign shell holds it — a "corporate inversion" — the company can sharply cut the U.S. taxes it owes while keeping its business, customers, and shareholders in America. This bill would treat such companies as domestic corporations for tax purposes, so they keep paying U.S. corporate taxes as if they had never left. It would even apply to deals already completed, reaching back to transactions after September 11, 2001, and to existing inverted companies starting with tax years after 2005.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary U.S. taxpayers, who otherwise pick up a larger share of the tax burden when profitable companies move their paper headquarters to low-tax countries; and U.S. companies that stay put, which currently compete against former compatriots with a lower tax bill.

how_it_helps.text: Redefines a company as domestic for tax purposes if a nominally foreign corporation acquires a U.S. company and the old owners end up holding most of the stock — the classic inversion structure — so the deal no longer removes the company from the U.S. tax system.

Applies a stricter 50 percent ownership test when the foreign shell has little real business in its home country and its stock mainly trades on U.S. markets, targeting paper moves to tax havens rather than genuine foreign operations.
Reaches partnerships and back-to-back step transactions, closing common restructuring routes, and applies retroactively to inversion deals completed after September 11, 2001.

analysis.who_pays: Shareholders and executives of U.S. multinational companies that had already inverted or planned to, who would owe U.S. taxes on income currently booked through foreign holding companies.

drawbacks.text: The tax applies retroactively to transactions completed after September 11, 2001, and to companies that inverted even earlier, which raises fairness concerns about changing tax rules for deals made under the old law.

It targets the inversion route but leaves the underlying U.S. system of taxing worldwide income untouched, so critics argued companies could still shift profits abroad through other means and the underlying competitive complaint would remain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core purpose — making a company pay U.S. taxes when its owners, operations, and stock market are all American — is sound and protects the tax base that funds services everyone relies on. The honest objections are the retroactive reach and the fact that it treats one symptom (paper headquarters moves) without fixing the profit-shifting incentives of the broader tax code. On balance, the public interest in a functioning corporate tax base outweighs the cost to companies that chose a tax-motivated flag change.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never held a hearing or vote on it, and it died there when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Neal of Massachusetts introduced the Corporate Patriot Enforcement Act of 2005 on September 29, 2005, joined by 10 Democratic cosponsors including Lloyd Doggett, Sander Levin, Rahm Emanuel, and Pete Stark.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, which was the last action ever recorded on it.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the bill's action history through the end of the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S. multinational companies that had inverted or could invert kept their lower foreign tax bills, and nothing changed for companies structuring new offshore deals.

for.name: Rep. Richard E. Neal
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: Rep. Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or committee vote; no action on the bill was recorded after its referral to his committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors were Democrats, but the bill never reached a vote, so the record shows no roll calls and no recorded Republican position on it.

industries.industry: U.S. multinational corporations using offshore holding companies
industries.note: The bill would treat inversion structures as domestic for tax purposes, restoring U.S. tax liability on companies that moved their paper headquarters to low-tax jurisdictions, including deals already completed. Their reduced U.S. tax payments shift the tax burden toward other taxpayers.

industries.industry: Tax-haven formation services (law, accounting, and trust firms)
industries.note: The bill counts series of related transactions as one and covers partnership routes, shrinking the market for restructuring packages built around offshore re-domiciling. The public interest in a full tax base runs against this industry's fee income.

industries.industry: U.S.-headquartered companies that did not invert
industries.note: Closing the inversion loophole reduces the competitive advantage former U.S. companies gained by shedding U.S. tax liability while competing in the same markets.
